analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the Medicare peer review system that checks whether billed care was needed.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to House committees and their health subcommittees in 1992, never got a hearing or vote, and died when that Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare's peer review system uses outside physician organizations to check whether services billed to Medicare were medically necessary and reasonably priced. This one-paragraph bill would erase that entire part of the law. Without it, Medicare would have no standing system of outside review of the quality and necessity of care billed by doctors and hospitals.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and other providers who bill Medicare would no longer face outside review of whether the care they billed was necessary, and they would be spared the appeals and recordkeeping the review system requires.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals part B of title XI of the Social Security Act, which is the Medicare Peer Review program, eliminating the entire system [S3].

The peer review program is the mechanism that uses review organizations to evaluate the medical necessity and quality of services billed to Medicare; repealing it would lift that oversight from Medicare providers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries would lose the standing outside check on whether billed care was medically necessary and properly performed, and the government would lose a tool for catching unnecessary or substandard care that taxpayers pay for.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the entire peer review program with no replacement, so Medicare would have no outside system for reviewing medical necessity or quality of care [S2] [S3].
The bill is a single repeal sentence with no accompanying findings or analysis, offering no explanation of what would take the review system's place [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers providers relief from oversight but provides nothing to offset the loss: no alternative quality-review mechanism, no savings tied to a stated purpose, and no protections for beneficiaries who want their billed care checked. Its one-sentence repeal leaves a hole where the review system used to be, so the cost falls on the people Medicare is supposed to protect.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then to their health subcommittees, and neither ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Duncan Jr. of Tennessee introduced the bill on July 29, 1992 [S1] [S5].
It was referred jointly to the House Committees on Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce, the two committees with jurisdiction over Medicare [S5].
Within a week it was sent down to each committee's health subcommittee, where it sat without action [S5].
Two Republican members cosponsored the bill [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one had to act to kill the bill; it simply expired in subcommittee. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers are no worse off than before, and providers who bill Medicare kept the review system rather than seeing it repealed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; the bill expired unused
